summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee, Anabel Eckerling, Boaz Israeli, Gali Yanovich, Ella Rosenne, Suzana Fichman-Horn, Ido Ben Zvi, Liat Sorski, Ronit Satchi-Fainaro, Tamar Geiger, Erica K Sloan, Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanisms behind the spontaneous regression of metastases following primary tumor (PT) excision, a phenomenon previously documented in case studies but lacking a mechanistic model. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-expressing MDA-MB-231 HM breast cancer model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor leads to a marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, while larger metastases remain unaffected. This regression is not due to surgical trauma, as sham surgery did not induce similar effects. Instead, the study identifies the primary tumor secretome as a critical support system for early metastatic growth. In vitro, tumor-conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and endothelial tube formation. In vivo, replenishing the secretome via osmotic minipumps after PT excision significantly diminished metastatic regression. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested micro-metastasis development even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, analysis of the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlate with poor patient survival (hazard ratio 2.05). These findings suggest that the primary tumor actively supports early metastatic niches via secreted factors, and that targeting these factors during the perioperative period could be a novel strategy to control minimal residual disease.

claims.description: Primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases.
The primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases.
Neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF arrests micro-metastasis development.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanisms behind the spontaneous regression of metastases following primary tumor (PT) excision, a phenomenon previously documented in case studies but lacking a mechanistic model. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-expressing MDA-MB-231 HM breast cancer model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor leads to a marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, while larger metastases remain unaffected. This regression is not due to surgical trauma, as sham surgery did not induce similar effects. Instead, the study identifies the primary tumor secretome as a critical support system for early metastatic growth. In vitro, tumor-conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and endothelial tube formation. In vivo, replenishing the secretome via osmotic minipumps after PT excision significantly diminished metastatic regression. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested micro-metastasis development even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, analysis of the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlate with poor patient survival (hazard ratio 2.05). These findings suggest that the primary tumor actively supports early metastatic niches via secreted factors, and that targeting these factors during the perioperative period could be a novel strategy to control minimal residual disease.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment. However, various case studies report the opposite effect; spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis. Unfortunately, postulated mechanisms have not been empirically tested, as no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The need to study potential interactions between the primary tumor (PT) and metastases is stressed by the current realization that the presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Herein, for the first time, we present an animal model of spontaneous regression of metastases following PT removal. We found that development of micro-metastases is supported by the numerous factors secreted from the PT. We hypothesized that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases. We hypothesized that if these four factors are among those that drive metastatic growth, their in vivo blockade would partly mimic the effect of primary tumor removal.

Methodological Details
A highly metastatic variant of the triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cell line, MDA-MB-231 HM, was transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were injected with 2×10 5 cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad. Once metastatic foci reached a total count of 10 6 photons/s (~ 3-4 weeks post injection), the primary tumor (average size of 80mm 3 ) was excised. CM was produced by incubating ~80% confluent MDA-MB-231 HM cells with serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C, 5% CO2. CM (and the same volume of SM as control) was then concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with either CM or SM and implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. Human Cytokine Array (R&D systems, Proteome Profiler TM Array, ARY022) was used to compare relative expression levels of 102 soluble human proteins. Mass spectrometry-based secretome analysis was performed using the Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer. Mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies were used to neutralize CXCL8/IL-8, Serpin E1/PAI-1, PDGF-AA, and MIF. Using the public TCGA provisional dataset (cBioPortal), we studied patient outcome in a lung adenocarcinoma cohort.

Procedures And Architectures
Primary tumor resection was performed under anesthesia with 2% isoflurane. For the sham surgery, an identical incision was made, however the PT was untouched. Cells were imaged for 8 hours, in 20 min intervals, using the IncuCyte system. Cells were incubated in CM or SM for 24 hrs, then washed and stained for AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD. Proteins were digested overnight with LysC/Trypsin mix and sequencing-grade modified Trypsin at room temperature. MS analysis was performed using a top10 method in which every high resolution MS scan was followed by fragmentation. Lung sections (6 μm) were stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E). Survival curve was conducted according to Kaplan Meier Analysis, and a hazard ratio was calculated in the R software.

Key Results
A dramatic decrease in metastatic signal, of up to 100-fold, was evident in mice along the 24 h following tumor excision, p<0.0001. These metastases have regressed into latent foci, as no increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases, p<0.000. Metastases regressed significantly following excision of the primary tumor, while continued to increase in mice subjected to sham surgery, p<0.05. Medium conditioned by MDA-MB-231 HM tumor cells enhanced viability, p<0.001 and adhesion, p<0.01 of cancer cells. Mice that were treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression than mice that received serum-free medium, p<0.005. We identified 28 cytokines that were highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Unbiased mass spectrometry proteomic analysis of CM identified 2,600 proteins, 359 of which were annotated as extracellular factors. Antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. High protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 and MIF were associated with significantly lower survival with a hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings of this study indicate a crucial supportive role for MDA-MB-231 HM tumor secretome in survival and progression of distant metastatic foci. Our findings suggest that tumor-secreted factors may act through multiple mechanisms to affect both malignant cells and/or their microenvironment. The findings provide an opportunity to empirically study metastatic regression into latent foci, and to explore mediating mechanisms. The primary tumor secretome can be a vital factor in promoting metastasis during early stages of metastatic formation.

Contradictions And Limitations
We herein tested only the combined effect of blocking four key secreted factors known to promote malignant progression. Other secreted factors are likely to also be involved in supporting metastatic progression. Different tumors, specifically syngeneic lines, should be similarly studied to test the generalizability of the novel phenomenon. The prevalence of post-operative regression of micro-metastases in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations.

Claims
Primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases. A dramatic decrease in metastatic signal, of up to 100-fold, was evident in mice along the 24 h following tumor excision. No increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases. 
The primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases. Mice that were treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression. Medium conditioned by MDA-MB-231 HM tumor cells enhanced viability and adhesion. Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression, potentially given their ability to secrete sufficient amount of the necessary factors. Targeting secreted factors could be a strategy to control minimal residual disease.
Neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF arrests micro-metastasis development. Antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression. High protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival. No difference in regression of metastases was evident between these two groups on post-excision day-1. These factors are crucial for survival of early stage micro-metastases.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
We identified 28 cytokines that were highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Unbiased mass spectrometry proteomic analysis of CM identified 2,600 proteins. Pathway enrichment analysis identified proteins engaged in key steps of metastasis including apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal following tumor excision. Figure 1E shows that regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases. Figure 2D shows that mice treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression. Figure 3B shows that antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression. Figure 3D shows that high protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of early micro-metastases. 3. The future path is to exploit the perioperative period to control minimal residual disease by targeting pro-metastatic factors.
